summary: Updates RFC 2460 to clarify how intermediate IPv6 nodes should handle extension headers, including ones defined in the future. It also specifies how extension headers are registered by IANA, with a minor update to RFC 2780.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 lets a packet carry extra headers between the fixed header and the transport header. Many firewalls drop such a packet when they meet a header type they do not know. This document tells forwarding devices to pass those packets on unless an administrator has deliberately chosen otherwise.

subtitle: Tells routers and firewalls not to drop IPv6 packets just because they carry extension headers the device does not know.

tldr.problem: Firewalls and other middleboxes often drop IPv6 packets carrying extension headers they do not recognise, which blocks newly standardised headers from ever being deployed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC clarifies that all forwarding nodes should pass packets regardless of extension headers, that discarding a standard header must be a configurable policy rather than an accident, and that IANA keeps a registry of extension header types.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 2460 and RFC 2780, but it does not change the underlying design of extension headers, so a new header may still fail on some paths until middleboxes are updated.

today: RFC 7045 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2013 that updates RFC 2460 and RFC 2780. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 7045 itself.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.content:
In IPv6, an extension header is any header that follows the initial 40 bytes of the packet and precedes the upper-layer header, which might be a transport header, an ICMPv6 header, or a notional 'No Next Header'. An initial set of extension headers was defined by RFC 2460, which also described how intermediate nodes should handle them, with the exception of the Hop-by-Hop Options header. The rule there was that extension headers are not examined or processed by any node along a packet's delivery path until the packet reaches the node identified in the Destination Address field of the IPv6 header.

That provision meant forwarding nodes should be completely transparent to extension headers. There was no provision for forwarding nodes to modify them, remove them, insert them, or use them to affect forwarding behaviour, so new extension headers could be introduced gradually and used only by hosts that had been updated to create and interpret them. Several new extension headers have been standardised since RFC 2460 was published.

IPv6 packets are not always forwarded by straightforward IP routing based on their first 40 bytes. Some routers, and a variety of intermediate nodes often referred to as middleboxes, such as firewalls, load balancers or packet classifiers, might inspect other parts of each packet, and such middlebox functions are often embedded in routers. Experience has shown that as a result the network is not transparent to IPv6 extension headers. Contrary to Section 4 of RFC 2460, middleboxes sometimes examine and process the entire IPv6 packet before deciding to forward or discard it, so they need to traverse the chain of extension headers, if present, until they find the transport header or an encrypted payload. Because not all IPv6 extension headers follow a uniform type-length-value format, this process is clumsy and requires knowledge of each header's format. The header chain may even be fragmented. The process is potentially slow as well as clumsy, possibly precluding its use in nodes attempting to process packets at line speed. This document does not intend to solve that problem, which is caused by the fundamental architecture of IPv6 extension headers.

If they encounter an unrecognised extension header type, some firewalls treat the packet as suspect and drop it. It is an established fact that several widely used firewalls do not recognise some or all of the extension headers standardised since RFC 2460 was published. Certain firewalls do not even handle all the extension headers standardised in RFC 2460, including the fragment header, causing fundamental problems of end-to-end connectivity. This applies in particular to firewalls that inspect packets at very high speed, since they cannot take the time to reassemble fragmented packets, especially under a denial-of-service attack. Other types of middlebox, such as load balancers or packet classifiers, might also fail in the presence of extension headers they do not recognise.

A contributory factor is that extension headers are numbered out of the existing IP Protocol Number space, so there is no collected list of them. It is hard for an implementor to quickly identify the full set of standard extension headers, and an implementor who consults only RFC 2460 will miss all extension headers defined subsequently.

Together these create a 'Catch-22' situation for the deployment of any newly standardised extension header except for local use. It cannot be widely deployed because existing middleboxes will drop it on many paths through the Internet, but most middleboxes will not be updated to allow the new header to pass until it has been proved safe and useful on the open Internet, which is impossible until the middleboxes have been updated. The uniform format now defined for extension headers will improve the situation, but only for future extensions.

The present document therefore clarifies that the requirement from RFC 2460 applies to all types of nodes that forward IPv6 packets and to all extension headers standardised now and in the future. It also requests that IANA create a subsidiary registry that clearly identifies extension header types, and updates RFC 2780 accordingly. Fundamental changes to the IPv6 extension header architecture are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Some firewalls drop a packet as soon as they meet a header type they do not know. That stops any new IPv6 header from being used, because no new header can work until every firewall on the path has learned it.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
Throughout the document, the term forwarding node refers to any router, firewall, load balancer, prefix translator, or any other device or middlebox that forwards IPv6 packets with or without examining the packet in any way.

Standard IPv6 extension headers are those specified in detail by IETF Standards Actions. Experimental extension headers include those defined by any Experimental RFC and the header values 253 and 254 defined by RFC 3692 and RFC 4727 when used as experimental extension headers. Defined extension headers are the standard extension headers plus the experimental ones.
sections.plainLanguage: A forwarding node is anything that passes an IPv6 packet along, whether or not it looks inside the packet. A standard header is one published through the normal IETF process; an experimental one is a trial that may change.

sections.title: Requirement to Transmit Extension Headers
sections.content:
Forwarding nodes that discard packets containing extension headers are known to cause connectivity failures and deployment problems, so it is important that forwarding nodes which inspect IPv6 headers be able to parse all defined extension headers and deal with them appropriately.

Any forwarding node along an IPv6 packet's path, which forwards the packet for any reason, SHOULD do so regardless of any extension headers that are present, as required by RFC 2460. Exceptionally, if a forwarding node is designed to examine extension headers for any reason, such as firewalling, it MUST recognise and deal appropriately with all standard IPv6 extension header types, and SHOULD recognise and deal appropriately with experimental IPv6 extension header types. The list of standard and experimental extension header types is maintained by IANA, and implementors are advised to check it regularly for updates.

RFC 2460 requires destination hosts to discard packets containing unrecognised extension headers. Intermediate forwarding nodes SHOULD NOT do this, since that might make them discard traffic using a recently standardised extension header they have not learned yet.

If a forwarding node discards a packet containing a standard IPv6 extension header, it MUST be the result of a configurable policy and not just the result of a failure to recognise such a header. The discard policy for each standard type of extension header MUST be individually configurable, and the default configuration SHOULD allow all standard extension headers. Experimental IPv6 extension headers SHOULD be treated in the same way, including an individually configurable discard policy, but the default configuration MAY drop them. Forwarding nodes MUST be configurable to allow packets containing unrecognised extension headers, though the default configuration MAY drop such packets.

The IPv6 Routing Header Types 0 and 1 have been deprecated, and Type 0 was deprecated by RFC 5095. This does not mean the IPv6 Routing Header can be unconditionally dropped by forwarding nodes. Packets containing standardised and undeprecated Routing Headers SHOULD be forwarded by default. At the time of writing these include Type 2, Type 3, and the experimental Routing Header Types 253 and 254. Others may be defined in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: A forwarding device should pass a packet on whatever extra headers it carries. If it does drop one, that has to be a choice the administrator made, not a side effect of the device not knowing the header.

sections.title: Hop-by-Hop Options
sections.content:
The IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options header SHOULD be processed by intermediate forwarding nodes as described in RFC 2460. However, it is to be expected that high-performance routers will either ignore it or assign packets containing it to a slow processing path. Designers planning to use a hop-by-hop option need to be aware of this likely behaviour.

As a reminder, in RFC 2460 it is stated that the Hop-by-Hop Options header, if present, must be first.
sections.plainLanguage: The header that tells routers what to do is the one most likely to be ignored, because handling it costs time. Anyone relying on it should expect fast routers to slow down or skip it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Forwarding nodes that operate as firewalls MUST conform to the requirements in the previous section in order to respect the IPv6 extension header architecture. In particular, packets containing standard extension headers are only to be discarded as a result of an intentionally configured policy.

These changes do not affect a firewall's ability to filter out traffic containing unwanted or suspect extension headers, if configured to do so. They do require firewalls to be capable of permitting any or all extension headers, if configured to do so. The default configurations are intended to allow normal use of any standard extension header, avoiding the connectivity issues described in Sections 1 and 2.1.

The default configuration might drop packets containing experimental extension headers. There is no header length field in an IPv6 header, and header types 253 and 254 might be used either for experimental extension headers or for experimental payload types. There is therefore no generic algorithm by which a firewall can distinguish the two cases and analyse the remainder of the packet. This should be considered when deciding on the appropriate default action for header types 253 and 254.

When new extension headers are standardised in the future, those implementing and configuring forwarding nodes, including firewalls, will need to take them into account. A newly defined header will exercise new code paths in a host that does recognise it, so caution may be required. Additional security issues with experimental values or new extension headers are to be found in RFC 4727 and RFC 6564. As a result, it is to be expected that the deployment process will be slow and will depend on satisfactory operational experience. Until deployment is complete, the new extension will fail in some parts of the Internet. This aspect needs to be considered when deciding to standardise a new extension, and specific security considerations for each new extension should be documented in the document that defines it.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall may still block headers it does not want, but only if someone has asked it to. The document also warns that every new header type means new code in the devices that understand it, so each one needs care.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has added an extra column titled 'IPv6 Extension Header' to the 'Assigned Internet Protocol Numbers' registry, to clearly mark those values that are also IPv6 extension header types defined by an IETF Standards Action or IESG Approval. This also applies to IPv6 extension header types defined in the future.

Additionally, IANA has closed the existing empty 'Next Header Types' registry to new entries and is redirecting its users to a new 'IPv6 Extension Header Types' registry, which contains only those protocol numbers that are also marked as IPv6 Extension Header types in the 'Assigned Internet Protocol Numbers' registry. Experimental values are marked as such. The references to the IPv6 Next Header field in RFC 2780 are to be interpreted as also applying to the IPv6 Extension Header field, and the new registry is managed accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA now keeps a separate list of the header types, so a device maker can look up one place and see every header it should know about.

viz.caption: WHERE AN EXTENSION HEADER SITS IN AN IPv6 PACKET (RFC 7045, SECTION 1)

layers.label: IPv6 header
layers.detail: The fixed 40 bytes at the start of the packet.

layers.label: Extension headers
layers.detail: Any header that follows the initial 40 bytes, such as a Hop-by-Hop Options or Routing header.

layers.label: Upper-layer header
layers.detail: A transport header, an ICMPv6 header, or a notional No Next Header.

viz.caption: THE RULES FOR FORWARDING NODES (RFC 7045, SECTION 2.1)

items.title: Forward by default
items.text: A forwarding node SHOULD forward a packet regardless of any extension headers present, as RFC 2460 requires.

items.title: Recognise the standard set
items.text: A node that inspects extension headers MUST recognise and handle all standard types, and SHOULD recognise experimental ones.

items.title: Only discard on purpose
items.text: Discarding a packet with a standard header MUST come from a configurable policy, with each header type individually configurable.

items.title: Allow what is unknown
items.text: Forwarding nodes MUST be configurable to allow unrecognised extension headers, though the default MAY drop them.

viz.caption: THE INITIAL IPV6 EXTENSION HEADER TYPES REGISTRY (RFC 7045, SECTION 4)

items.label: Routing Header for IPv6
items.desc: Defined by RFC 2460; Type 0 deprecated by RFC 5095.
